title: Magnus effect
description: A spinning ball moving through air curves sideways, because its spin drags the air faster past one side than the other. It's why a sliced ball swerves, and it drove ships with tall spinning cylinders for sails.
effect: a spinning object moving through air is pushed sideways
pickWhy: A clear, named effect with real uses (rotor ships, curveballs, flettner rotors) and plenty still untried.

title: Electrocapillarity
description: A voltage changes how well a liquid wets a surface: a drop of mercury in acid flattens or bulges as the voltage is turned up and down. Today it pushes droplets around lab chips and focuses liquid lenses.
effect: a voltage makes a drop spread out or bead up
pickWhy: The database calls it electrowetting, which took off in the 1990s; I dated it to Lippmann's 1875 discovery and renamed it to match.

title: Pockels effect
description: An electric field changes how strongly certain crystals bend light, in step with the field. Crystals that switch light this way put data onto optical fibres and fire the pulses of many lasers.
effect: an electric field changes how a crystal bends light
pickWhy: Named effect, clear job (switching light), already behind real inventions the deck lacks.

title: Vortex cooling
description: Compressed air whirled inside a tube splits into a hot stream out one end and a cold stream out the other, with no moving parts. Factories use vortex tubes to cool cutting tools and electrical cabinets.
effect: whirling compressed air splits into a hot stream and a cold stream
pickWhy: Borderline: the vortex tube is itself an invention, so the effect and the device share a name. I kept the effect and left the tube as a possible invention card.

title: Sagnac effect
description: Two light beams sent opposite ways round a spinning loop come back out of step, by an amount set by how fast it spins. Aircraft and submarines steer by ring-laser gyroscopes that measure it.
effect: light sent both ways round a turning loop comes back out of step
pickWhy: A named effect with a big job (navigation without stars or satellites).

title: Skin effect
description: Fast alternating current crowds into the outer skin of a wire, the more so the faster it alternates. That's why radio aerials can be hollow tubes, and why induction furnaces harden only the surface of steel.
effect: fast-alternating current flows only in a conductor's outer skin
pickWhy: Mostly a nuisance, but it does jobs (surface hardening, shielding).

title: Triboluminescence
description: Some crystals flash light when crushed, scratched or pulled apart: crunch a lump of sugar in the dark and it sparks blue. Coatings that glow where they're strained can show cracks in bridges and wings.
effect: some crystals give off light when crushed or strained
pickWhy: Renamed from the database's umbrella term to the oldest named form; Bacon described sugar sparking in 1605.

title: Negative thermal expansion
description: Some materials shrink when heated: zirconium tungstate contracts steadily from near absolute zero to 700 °C. Mixed into other materials it cancels out their swelling, for mirrors and fillings that keep their shape.
effect: a material that shrinks when it's heated
pickWhy: Borderline on the date: water shrinking as it warms from 0 to 4 °C was known centuries earlier; I dated it to the 1996 material that made it useful.

title: Electric wind
description: Air near a sharp point at high voltage becomes charged and is pushed away, making a breeze with no moving parts. It runs silent air purifiers, and in 2018 it flew a model plane with no propeller.
effect: a sharp point at high voltage blows a breeze
pickWhy: Old, named, simple, and the future-tech kind: lots of jobs not yet done by it.

title: Casimir effect
description: Two metal plates a hair's breadth apart in a vacuum are pushed together by the restless energy of empty space. The force is tiny, but it makes the parts of micromachines stick.
effect: empty space pushes two very close plates together
pickWhy: Borderline: famous and real, but far too weak to do any job at a useful size. Drop unless you want effects for far-future candidates.

title: Kaye effect
description: A thin stream of shampoo poured onto a puddle of itself can suddenly leap back up as a bouncing jet. It happens only in liquids that thin out when stirred.
effect: a stream of shampoo leaps back off its own puddle
pickWhy: A curiosity with no job.

title: Second sound
description: In superfluid helium, heat travels as a wave, like sound, instead of slowly spreading out. It was predicted by Tisza and Landau and measured in Moscow.
effect: heat travels as a wave in superfluid helium
pickWhy: Works only in liquid helium a couple of degrees above absolute zero.

title: Sound
effect: pressure waves travel through air, water or solids
pickWhy: Too general: a whole field, not one effect. The deck already has Acoustics.

title: Radiation
effect: energy travels as waves or particles
pickWhy: Too general.

title: Freezing
effect: a liquid turns solid when cooled
pickWhy: An everyday process, not a discovery with a date.

title: Vacuum
effect: a space emptied of air
pickWhy: A condition, not an effect; and the deck already has Air pumps and Early pneumatics.

title: Lever
effect: a bar on a pivot trades distance for force
pickWhy: A machine, not a phenomenon; the deck already has Lever mathematics.

title: Möbius strip
effect: a loop with a half twist has only one side
pickWhy: Already a card; nothing to add.

title: Shapes of constant width
description: A shape need not be a circle to be the same width in every direction: a rounded triangle rolls a board as smoothly as a wheel. Such shapes make drills that cut square holes and coins that vending machines can measure.
effect: a non-round shape has the same width in every direction
pickWhy: Borderline: a shape, not a physical effect. But shapes do jobs (Möbius belts, Reuleaux drills), so this is your call on whether geometry counts.

title: Holes
effect: an opening lets things through
pickWhy: Not a phenomenon.

title: Forced convection
effect: a fan or pump carries heat away in moving fluid
pickWhy: One of four convection variants in the database (forced, free, mixed, Rayleigh-Bénard). Merge them into one Convection card.

title: Piezoelectric effect
effect: squeezing a crystal makes a voltage, and a voltage makes it flex
pickWhy: Already a card (Piezoelectricity); just link the database entry to it.

title: Bernoulli's principle
description: Where a flowing liquid or gas speeds up, its pressure drops. It's why a perfume atomiser sprays, a carburettor sucks in fuel, and a shower curtain billows inward.
effect: a fluid's pressure drops where it flows faster
pickWhy: Borderline: the deck's Kinetic gases card is from the same 1738 book by the same author, but it's about a different effect, so this gets its own card.

title: Flocculation
description: A pinch of a salt like alum makes the fine particles clouding muddy water clump into flakes that sink, leaving it clear. Schulze showed the salt's charge decides how little is needed. Every water works does this.
effect: a salt makes fine suspended particles clump and sink
pickWhy: Borderline on the date: alum has cleared water since antiquity; I dated it to when the effect was explained.

title: Hygroscopy
description: Some salts pull so much water from the air that they dissolve into a puddle of their own brine. Packets of silica gel and the salt on winter roads work this way.
effect: some substances pull water out of the air
pickWhy: Borderline: a useful effect, but known since antiquity with no clear discoverer or date. Renamed from Deliquescence to the broader effect.
